newsitem.title: USA: Connecticut hails U.S. court ruling on tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: Connecticut hails U.S. court ruling on tobacco suit.

text.p: Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal Thursday hailed a federal court decision allowing the state to press ahead with a $1 billion lawsuit to recover money spent to treat smoking-related illnesses.
But a lawyer for the maker of Marlboro cigarettes warned there were still "light years" to go in the court fight.
Connecticut is one of at least 19 states trying to recoup the costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.

Federal Judge Peter Dorsey in New Haven, Conn., on Monday dismissed a lawsuit filed by four tobacco companies seeking to block Connecticut's suit, which also seeks to halt aggressive marketing of tobacco products to children and teen-agers, Blumenthal said.
The tobacco companies filed their suit on June 28 in an attempted pre-emptive strike against the state's suit, which was filed on July 18, said a source involved in the case.
Blumenthal said Dorsey's ruling was the first time a federal judge has dismissed this type of tobacco industry action against a state.

He called the ruling a major win for Connecticut's effort to halt marketing of tobacco products to children and end other practices that have caused the state to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to pay for tobacco-related illnesses.

"This decision, which explicitly recognizes the principle that the federal government should not interfere with legitimate state functions, clears the way for our case to continue," Blumenthal said in a statement.
"These four companies attempted to use the federal courts to pre-empt our lawsuit and their efforts have been resoundingly rejected," Blumenthal said.
The industry's suit was filed by Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the world's largest cigarette maker, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co., and Lorillard Tobacco.
Connecticut's suit against the companies and three related organizations alleges violations of the state's antitrust and unfair trade laws and other claims.
A tobacco company lawyer shrugged off the ruling.
"The attorney general's excitement is misplaced and profoundly premature," said Michael York, an attorney for Philip Morris, which makes Marlboro and other brands.
"He knows that there are still light years to go in this lawsuit, and that innumerable legal hurdles await him."
Philip Morris and other companies may appeal the judge's ruling, York said.
Wall Street analysts also downplayed the decision.
"The attorney general has made some flamboyant comments, but let's see what happens when it's all said and done," said David Adelman at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"It's still very early days. Ultimately, these (state) suits are about PR and politics," he said.

"We're still waiting for much more important decisions on cases in Florida and Mississippi," said Allan Kaplan, tobacco analyst at Merrill Lynch. "The big decision will be whether these cases can be tried as a class or must be reviewed individually, as the tobacco companies want."
